as_told.title: Atlantis destroyed by Meltwater Pulse 1B flood

tellings.quote: Let me begin by observing first of all, that nine thousand was the sum of years which had elapsed since the war which was said to have taken place between those who dwelt outside the pillars of Heracles and all who dwelt within them; this war I am going to describe.
Many great deluges have taken place during the nine thousand years, for that is the number of years which have elapsed since the time of which I am speaking;

As touching your citizens of 9000 years ago, I will briefly inform you of their laws and of their most famous action; the exact particulars of the whole we will hereafter go through at our leisure in the sacred registers themselves.

But afterwards there occurred violent earthquakes and floods; and in a single day and night of misfortune all your warlike men in a body sank into the earth, and the island of Atlantis in like manner disappeared in the depths of the sea.

Now the day was that day of the Apaturia which is called the Registration of Youth, at which, according to custom, our parents gave prizes for recitations, and the poems of several poets were recited by us boys, and many of us sang the poems of Solon, which at that time had not gone out of fashion.

plain: The ancient Greek philosopher Plato dates the sinking of Atlantis, an island said to have vanished into the sea, to 9,000 years before the Athenian lawmaker Solon heard the tale in Egypt. The researcher Randall Carlson tells Michels that Solon's visit came around 600 BC, which puts the date near 9600 BC, the end of the last ice age, and Michels, crediting Carlson and the writer Graham Hancock, goes further on later shows: he says the flood that ended the ice age, which he calls Meltwater Pulse 1B, is what drowned Atlantis. In Plato's dialogues the Timaeus and Critias, read in Benjamin Jowett's translation, an Egyptian priest tells Solon of "your citizens of 9000 years ago" and says that "afterwards there occurred violent earthquakes and floods" in which Atlantis "disappeared in the depths of the sea," but the texts give no date BC and say nothing of an ice age, and in the Critias the nine thousand years run back from Critias's own day, with "many great deluges" along the way rather than a single flood.

discussion.text: In Jowett's translation of the Critias, Critias counts the nine thousand years back from his own day to the war, not from Solon's visit to Egypt, and speaks of "many great deluges" during those years rather than one flood.

In Jowett's translation of the Timaeus, the 9000 years are counted by the Egyptian priest speaking to Solon ("As touching your citizens of 9000 years ago"), back to the Athenians who fought Atlantis, and the "violent earthquakes and floods" that sank the island came "afterwards"; the date of 600 BC for Solon's visit is the tellers', and the festival in the text, "the Apaturia", is where the elder Critias told the tale to the younger, generations after Solon. Matching the 9000 years to the end of the ice age and to Meltwater Pulse 1B is the tellers' step from the text's count, which the text neither states nor excludes.
